slots.text: But I break off here. I am no poet, and I go about things only dialectically. First, it should be noted that the hero receives this information at the decisive moment. He is therefore pure and has nothing to repent of; he has not bound himself frivolously to his beloved. Second, he has a divine pronouncement on his side — or rather against him — so he is not steered by his own cleverness, as those slender lovers, men and women alike, are. It further goes without saying that the pronouncement makes him just as unhappy as the bride — indeed a little more so, since he is, after all, the occasion of it. For it is true that the augurs foretold a misfortune only for him; but the question is whether this misfortune might not be such that, when it strikes him, it also strikes their happiness as husband and wife. What, then, is he to do? 1) Should he keep silent and hold the wedding, thinking: perhaps the misfortune will not come right away; at any rate I have stood up for love and have not been afraid of making myself unhappy — but I must keep silent, for otherwise even the short moment is thrown away? This seems plausible, but it is nothing of the kind; for in that case he has offended against the girl. By his silence he has in a way made the girl guilty; for had she known, she would presumably never have agreed to such a match. In the hour of distress, then, he will have to carry not merely the misfortune but also the responsibility for his having kept silent: her just anger that he kept silent. 2) Should he keep silent and refrain from holding the wedding? In that case he must enter into a mystification — a deliberate deception — by which he annihilates himself in his relation to her. Aesthetics might perhaps approve of this. The catastrophe could then be shaped like the actual one, except that at the very last moment there would be an explanation — one that came too late all the same, since, aesthetically considered, it becomes a necessity to let him die, unless this science should find itself able to cancel that ill-fated prophecy. Yet this conduct, however magnanimous it may be, contains an offense against the girl and the reality of her love. 3) Should he speak? One must not forget, of course, that our hero is a little too poetic for the renouncing of his love to mean no more to him than a failed business speculation. If he speaks, the whole thing becomes an unhappy love story in the same style as Axel and Valborg. The two become a pair that heaven itself parts. In the present case, though, this separation has to be thought of somewhat differently, since it also results from the free act of the individuals. For what is so very difficult about the dialectic of this case is that the misfortune is to strike only him. So they do not, like Axel and Valborg, get a common expression for their suffering, whereas heaven parts Axel and Valborg alike, since they stand equally near to each other. If that were the case here, a way out could be imagined. For since heaven uses no visible power to separate them but leaves it to the lovers themselves, it would surely be conceivable that they might resolve together to defy heaven, misfortune and all.

notes.anchorAfterEn: in the same style as Axel and Valborg.
notes.text: Incidentally, from this point one could set off in another direction of dialectical movements. Heaven foretells a misfortune for him from his marriage. So he could, of course, refrain from holding the wedding without therefore giving up the girl, and live with her in a romantic union that, for the lovers, would be more than reassuring. This, however, contains an offense against the girl, because he does not, in his love for her, express the universal. It would nevertheless be a task both for a poet and for an ethicist who wanted to defend marriage. In general, if poetry became attentive to the religious and to the inwardness of individuality, it would find far more significant tasks than those it busies itself with now. Over and over, after all, one hears this story in poetry: a man is tied to one girl he once loved — or perhaps never properly loved — because now he has seen another girl, who is the ideal. A man gets it wrong in life: the street was right, but it was the wrong house, for across the way, on the second floor, lives the ideal — this, people think, is a task for poetry. A lover has made a mistake: he saw his beloved by lamplight and thought she had dark hair, but look! on closer inspection it was fair — but her sister, she is the ideal. This, people think, is a task for poetry. My opinion is that every such man is a Laban (a boor) who may be unbearable enough in life but ought to be hissed off at once when he tries to make himself important in poetry. Only passion against passion makes a poetic collision, not this rattling-about of particularities within one and the same passion. If, for instance, a girl in the Middle Ages falls in love and then satisfies herself that earthly love is a sin, and prefers a heavenly love, then there is a poetic collision here, and the girl is poetic, because her life is in the idea.

slots.text: Ethics, however, will require of him that he speak. His heroic courage must then essentially consist in giving up the aesthetic magnanimity — which in casu (in this case), it is true, could hardly be thought to contain any admixture of the vanity that lies in being concealed, since it must surely be clear to him that he is making the girl unhappy all the same. The reality of this heroic courage, however, depends on its having first had its presupposition and then cancelled it. For otherwise one could get heroes enough, especially in our time — our time, which has carried to an unrivalled virtuosity the forgery that achieves the highest by skipping over the middle term.

But what is this sketch for, then, since I still get no further than the tragic hero? Because it was still possible that it might throw some light on the paradox. Everything depends, then, on how he stands in relation to the augurs’ pronouncement, which in one way or another becomes decisive for his life. Is this pronouncement publici juris — public property — or is it a privatissimum — a private lesson? The scene is Greece, and an augur’s pronouncement is intelligible to everyone. I do not mean only that the single individual can understand its content lexically; I mean that the single individual can understand that an augur is announcing heaven’s decision to the single individual. So the augur’s pronouncement is intelligible not only to the hero but to everyone, and no private relation to the deity results from it. He can do what he likes; what has been foretold will happen; and neither by acting nor by refraining does he come into a closer relation to the deity or become the object either of its grace or of its wrath. Any individual will be able to understand the outcome just as well as the hero, and there is no secret writing legible to the hero alone. Insofar as he wants to speak, then, he can do so perfectly well, for he can make himself understood. Insofar as he wants to keep silent, it is because, by virtue of being the single individual, he wants to be higher than the universal — wants to delude himself with all kinds of fantastic notions about how she will soon forget this business, and so on. If, on the other hand, heaven’s will had not been announced to him by an augur — if it had come to his knowledge entirely privately, if it had placed itself in an entirely private relation to him — then we are at the paradox, if it exists at all (for my deliberation proceeds by dilemma). In that case he could not speak, no matter how much he wanted to. He would then not be enjoying himself in his silence; he would be suffering the pain — but that pain would be precisely his assurance that he was justified. His silence would then not be grounded in his wanting, as the single individual, to place himself in an absolute relation to the universal, but in his having been placed, as the single individual, in an absolute relation to the absolute. He would then also be able to find rest in it, as far as I can imagine, whereas his magnanimous silence would be constantly troubled by the demands of the ethical. It is altogether to be wished that aesthetics would for once try to begin where for so many years it has ended: at illusory magnanimity. The moment it did that, it would be playing straight into the hands of the religious; for this power is the only one that can rescue the aesthetic from its struggle with the ethical. Queen Elizabeth sacrifices her love for Essex to the state by signing his death warrant. This was a heroic deed, even if a little personal offense was in play too — that he had not sent her the ring. As is well known, he had in fact sent it, but it had been held back through the malice of a lady at court. Elizabeth, so the story goes — ni fallor (unless I am mistaken) — received word of this; then she sat for ten days with one finger in her mouth, biting it without saying a single word, and then she died. That would be a task for a poet who knew how to wrench the mouth open; otherwise it is at most of use to a ballet master, with whom the poet in our time often enough confuses himself.

Now I will follow this with a sketch in the direction of the demonic. For this I can use the legend of Agnete and the merman. The merman is a seducer who shoots up from his hiding place in the abyss and, in wild lust, seizes and breaks the innocent flower that stood in all her grace on the shore, pensively bowing her head to the murmur of the sea. This is how the poets have seen it up to now. Let us make a change. The merman was a seducer. He has called to Agnete; with his smooth talk he has coaxed out what was hidden in her; in the merman she has found what she was seeking, what she had been staring down at the bottom of the sea to find. Agnete wants to go with him. The merman has lifted her onto his arm; Agnete twines herself about his neck; trustingly, with her whole soul, she gives herself to the stronger one. He is already standing at the water’s edge; he is leaning out over the sea to plunge down with his prey — then Agnete looks at him once more: not fearfully, not doubtingly, not proud of her happiness, not drunk with desire, but in absolute faith, but in absolute humility, like the lowly flower she thought herself to be; with this look, in absolute trust, she confides her whole destiny to him. — And look! The sea no longer roars; its wild voice falls silent; the passion of nature, which is the merman’s strength, deserts him; the sea falls dead calm — and still Agnete looks at him in this way. Then the merman collapses. He cannot resist the power of innocence; his own element proves faithless to him; he cannot seduce Agnete. He leads her home again and explains to her that all he wanted was to show her how beautiful the sea was when calm; and Agnete believes him. — Then he goes back alone, and the sea rages, but the despair in the merman rages more wildly. He can seduce Agnete, he can seduce a hundred Agnetes, he can bewitch any girl — but Agnete has triumphed, and the merman has lost her. She can become his only as prey; faithfully he can belong to no girl, since he is, after all, only a merman. I have allowed myself a small change in the merman; basically I have changed Agnete a little too. For in the legend Agnete is not altogether without guilt — just as, in general, it is nonsense and gallantry and an offense against womankind to conceive of a seduction where the girl has no, no, no guilt at all. In the legend Agnete is — to put it in slightly more modern terms — a woman who demands the interesting, and any woman of that kind can always count on a merman being close by; for mermen spot that sort of thing with half an eye and make for it as the shark makes for its prey. It is therefore very stupid — or else it is a rumor that a merman has had put about — to say that so-called cultivation protects a girl against seduction. No, existence is more just and more even-handed than that: there is only one means, and that is innocence.

notes.text: That legend could also be treated in another way. The merman does not want to seduce Agnete, even though he has seduced many before. He is no longer a merman — or, if you like, he is a poor wretch of a merman who has long been sitting on the bottom of the sea, grieving. Yet he knows, as the legend does teach, that an innocent girl’s love can save him. But his conscience is bad where girls are concerned, and he does not dare approach them. Then he sees Agnete. Many times already, hidden in the reeds, he has watched her walking along the shore. Her beauty, her quiet absorption in herself, hold him captive to her; but all is melancholy in his soul, and no wild lust stirs in it. And when the merman mingles his sigh with the whispering of the reeds, she turns her ear that way, stands still and sinks into dreams — lovelier than any woman, and yet beautiful as a saving angel who inspires trust in the merman. The merman takes courage; he approaches Agnete, he wins her love, he hopes for his salvation. But Agnete was no quiet girl. She was very fond of the roaring of the sea, and the melancholy sigh by the water pleased her only because it made the roaring within her the stronger. She wants to be off, off — to storm wildly out into the infinite with the merman she loves — then she inflames the merman. She scorned his humility; now pride awakes. And the sea roars, and the wave froths, and the merman clasps Agnete in his arms and hurls himself into the abyss with her. He had never been so wild, never so full of craving; for it was through this girl that he had hoped to be saved. He soon grew tired of Agnete; yet her body was never found, for she became a mermaid who tempted men with her songs.

slots.text: We will now endow the merman with a human consciousness, and let the fact that he is a merman stand for a previous human existence, in whose consequences his life was entangled. Nothing prevents him from becoming a hero; for the step he now takes is a reconciling one. He is saved by Agnete; the seducer is crushed; he has bowed before the power of innocence; he can never seduce again. But in the same instant two powers contend for him: repentance; and Agnete and repentance. If repentance alone takes him, he is concealed; if Agnete and repentance take him, he is disclosed.

Now, insofar as repentance seizes the merman and he remains concealed, he has certainly made Agnete unhappy. For Agnete loved him in all her innocence. She believed it was the truth that at that moment — when he seemed changed even to her, however well he hid it — he only wanted to show her the beautiful stillness of the sea. Yet the merman himself becomes, as regards passion, still more unhappy; for he loved Agnete with a great many passions, and he had, besides, a new guilt to bear. The demonic in repentance will now no doubt explain to him that just this is his punishment — and the more it tortures him, the better.

If he gives himself over to this demonic element, he perhaps makes one more attempt to save Agnete, in the way that one can, in a certain sense, save a person with the help of evil. He knows that Agnete loves him. If he could wrest this love from Agnete, she would in a way be saved. But how? The merman is too sensible to count on an open-hearted confession arousing her disgust. So perhaps he will try to stir up all the dark passions in her — to scorn her, mock her, make her love ridiculous and, if possible, goad her pride. He will spare himself no torment; for this is the profound contradiction in the demonic — and in a certain sense a demonic person has infinitely more good dwelling in him than trivial people have. The more selfish Agnete is, the easier it will be to deceive her (for only very inexperienced people think that innocence is easy to deceive; existence is exceedingly profound, and the easiest thing for the clever is to fool the clever) — but the more terrible the merman’s sufferings will be. The more cunningly his deception is laid out, the less will Agnete’s modesty lead her to hide her suffering from him. She will use every means, and they will not be without effect either — not, that is, in shaking him, but in torturing him.
